about: Report scoring eval. Each case is a finished mock interview with answers of known quality. Transcript turns: q = main question, f = follow-up, a = candidate answer, close = interviewer closing. Expectations are score bands, not exact numbers.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Priya. Tell me about the most complex system migration you've led.

transcript.a: The wallet ledger migration at PhonePe. The monolith was our biggest outage risk: a single Postgres primary took every wallet write. I owned the design and led 11 engineers over 18 months. I split it into 6 services around clear ownership boundaries, and the hard part was moving money without double-spend. We ran dual writes behind a feature flag, reconciled old and new ledgers every hour, and only cut over a merchant cohort once reconciliation showed zero mismatches for 7 days. We finished with zero data loss, and write latency went from 180 to 60 milliseconds at p99. The trade-off I'd call out: dual writes doubled our ops load for about 4 months, which I accepted because a big-bang cutover on money was not a risk I'd take.

transcript.f: How did you handle a mismatch when reconciliation did find one?

transcript.a: We had 3 real mismatches. Each froze that cohort's cutover automatically. For one, a retry storm had created duplicate debit events; we traced it to a missing idempotency key on one client path. I added idempotency keys at the API gateway so every write path had one, backfilled the 212 affected entries with finance signing off, and added the case to our reconciliation test suite so it couldn't regress.

transcript.q: How do you decide between building for scale now versus later?

transcript.a: I size against the next 18 months of real load, not a hypothetical. For the payment APIs I designed at PhonePe, we projected 30k requests per second at peak and built for 45k with idempotent, stateless handlers so we could scale horizontally. What I don't do is add sharding or new datastores before the numbers need them. At Flipkart I pushed back on sharding the order database a year early; we added read replicas instead, which held through Big Billion Days at 99.99% availability and saved about 6 months of work.

transcript.q: Tell me about a time you reduced cost without hurting reliability.

transcript.a: Our Kafka and Cassandra clusters were sized for a peak that happened 4 days a year. I led an audit of utilisation per topic and table, and found average CPU at 11%. We moved to autoscaling consumer groups, tiered storage for older Kafka data, and right-sized Cassandra nodes after load-testing at 1.5x peak. Cost dropped 32%, about 2.1 crore rupees a year, and we had no reliability regressions over the next two sale events. I made the rollback plan the first deliverable, so every step could be undone in under 10 minutes.

transcript.close: That's all from me. Thanks, Vikram.

cases.why: Relevant but thin: says 'we' instead of 'I', no numbers, skips part of the question. Should land in the middle, not the top.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Daniel. Walk me through a service you built and your role in it.

transcript.a: At Razorpay we built a reconciliation service for UPI. It matches our records with the bank's records. We used Go and Postgres. It was a big improvement on the old system, which was slow. The team worked on it for a few months and it went well.

transcript.f: What did you personally own, and how did you measure the improvement?

transcript.a: I worked on a lot of the backend parts. It was faster after we launched, the dashboards looked much better, and the ops team was happy with it.

transcript.q: Tell me about a production incident you handled.

transcript.a: There was an incident where settlements were delayed. We looked at the logs and found a problem with one of the jobs, so we fixed it and restarted it. After that we added some monitoring so it wouldn't happen again. It took a few hours to resolve.

transcript.q: How would you design a rate limiter for a payments API?

transcript.a: I would use Redis to keep a counter per user or per API key, and if the count goes over a limit in a time window we return a 429. The window could be something like one minute. That's a common approach and it works well.

transcript.close: Thanks, that's the end of our session.

cases.why: The core honesty rule: generic, buzzword answers with no specifics must never score above 5/10.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Meera. Tell me about a time you took ownership of something difficult.

transcript.a: I always take ownership of my work. I'm a very responsible person and I believe in giving 100 percent. Whenever something difficult comes up, I make sure it gets done. My managers have always appreciated my ownership.

transcript.q: Describe a disagreement with a teammate and how you resolved it.

transcript.a: I'm a team player, so I don't really have conflicts. If there's a disagreement I listen to everyone and we find the best solution together. Communication is key.

transcript.q: What's a mistake you made and what did you learn?

transcript.a: Sometimes I work too hard and take on too much. I learned that it's important to balance things and to ask for help when needed. Now I manage my time better.

cases.why: Non-answers ('I don't know', 'can we skip') should score at the very bottom.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Sofia. Tell me about a project you're proud of.

transcript.a: So I think the project I'm most proud of is really about the journey more than the destination, you know. In my career I've worked on many different kinds of systems and each one taught me something valuable. What I've found is that the most important thing is to understand the business requirements deeply, align with stakeholders, and make sure that the technical solution is robust, scalable and maintainable. I always try to follow best practices, write clean code, and think about the long-term impact of every decision. It's also really about collaboration, because no project succeeds without a great team, and I've been lucky to work with amazing people. Overall I would say it was a very successful project that delivered a lot of value to the organisation and to our customers, and I learned a lot from it.

transcript.q: How do you approach debugging a production issue?

transcript.a: Debugging is honestly one of my favourite parts of engineering because it's like being a detective. My approach is very holistic. First I try to stay calm, because panicking never helps anyone. Then I try to understand the full picture, look at all the relevant information, and think about what could possibly be going wrong. I believe in being methodical and systematic, and also in communicating clearly with everyone involved so that stakeholders are aware. After it's resolved I always think about lessons learned and how we can prevent similar issues in the future, because continuous improvement is really important to me.

transcript.close: Thanks, that's the end of our time.

cases.why: Per-answer discrimination inside one interview: strong answers high, the vague one capped.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Rahul. Tell me about something you built that you're proud of.

transcript.a: The UPI reconciliation service at Razorpay. Reconciliation ran as a nightly batch and took 5 hours, so mismatches were found a day late. I rewrote the matching step in Go as a streaming job and personally owned the design and rollout. I added a hash index on the bank reference and processed files in parallel chunks. Batch time went from 5 hours to 40 minutes, and p95 latency on the lookup API dropped from 900 to 540 milliseconds. I ran it in shadow mode for 2 weeks and compared outputs line by line before switching over.

transcript.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.

transcript.a: I don't really disagree with managers much. I think it's important to respect their decisions and I usually go with what the team thinks is best.

transcript.q: How did you scale the settlement jobs?

transcript.a: Settlements ran as cron jobs on one machine, and at around 800k transactions a day they started missing the bank cutoff. I proposed moving them to Kafka consumers partitioned by merchant, and I built the consumer group and the retry path with idempotency keys so reprocessing a message could never pay twice. We scaled to 2M transactions a day with zero missed settlements over 6 months, and I wrote the runbook for the on-call team.

cases.why: Same decent answers as the next case, judged at fresher level. Must score higher than when judged as senior.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Hannah. Tell me about an analysis you did that led to a decision.

transcript.a: At my Zomato internship I built a Power BI dashboard for restaurant churn across 3 cities. While building it I noticed churned restaurants often had slow deliveries, so I checked it in SQL: 18% of churned restaurants had average delivery times above 45 minutes, compared with 6% of active ones. I presented this to my manager, and the Jaipur team ran a pilot to prioritise riders for those restaurants.

transcript.q: How would you figure out why orders dropped 10% in a city last week?

transcript.a: First I'd check whether the drop is real and not a data issue, like a missing day in the pipeline. Then I'd split it: new versus repeat customers, by area, by restaurant category, and by time of day, to find where the drop is concentrated. I'd also look for outside causes like rain, a competitor's discount, or an app release. Once I knew where it was, I'd talk to the city team to confirm the reason.

transcript.q: Tell me about a time you worked with limited data.

transcript.a: For the canteen forecast project we only had one semester of handwritten sales records. I typed them into Excel, used a simple moving average by weekday, and adjusted for exam weeks. It wasn't perfect, but the canteen used it to plan quantities and food waste went down 22% over the semester.

cases.why: Identical answers to the previous case, judged against a senior bar. Must score clearly lower (scores are relative to level).
A fresher with well-structured, quantified answers from college work. Level-appropriate strength must be rewarded.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Kabir. Tell me about a time you had to influence someone without authority.

transcript.a: As Finance Club treasurer I managed a 4 lakh rupee budget, and the events team wanted to spend 60% of it on one fest. I didn't have authority to block it, so I built a one-page sheet showing last year's spend per event against attendance: the fest cost 3 times more per attendee than our workshops. I shared it with the president and the events lead before the meeting, suggested we cap the fest at 40% and move the rest to two workshops, and they agreed. Workshop attendance that year went from 90 to 210 people.

transcript.q: Tell me about a mistake you made and what you changed.

transcript.a: In my Zomato internship I sent a churn number to 12 city managers that double-counted restaurants that had closed and reopened. A manager in Pune spotted it the next day. I owned it: I sent a correction within the hour, explained the cause, and added a deduplication step and a row-count check to the SQL before every refresh. After that I also had my manager review any new metric before it went out, and there were no more errors for the rest of the internship.

cases.why: Two main questions with a follow-up each: the report must have exactly one entry per main question.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Priya. Tell me about the order-tracking API you built at Swiggy.

transcript.a: It was an internal API in FastAPI that returned the live status of an order. I built most of the endpoints and the caching layer.

transcript.f: What was the latency and how did you get there?

transcript.a: Median response was 120 milliseconds. I added Redis caching for order status with a 5 second TTL, because status changes rarely inside that window, and that took most calls off Postgres.

transcript.q: How do you make sure a settlement job never pays a merchant twice?

transcript.a: Each payout gets an idempotency key made from the merchant ID and settlement date. Before paying, the job checks if that key was already processed.

transcript.f: What if the job crashes after paying but before recording the key?

transcript.a: Then you'd pay twice with that design. You'd need to record the intent first in the same transaction, or use the bank's idempotency support. I'd have to think about the exact approach.

cases.why: Technical content correctness: fluent but factually wrong answers must score low.

transcript.q: Hi, I'm Daniel. What does a database index do, and what does it cost?

transcript.a: An index makes every query faster, reads and writes, and it doesn't cost anything, so the best practice is to index every column. That's what I always do at Razorpay.

transcript.q: Is HTTP stateful or stateless, and why does it matter for scaling?

transcript.a: HTTP is stateful because the server keeps a connection per user for the whole session. That's why you can only scale an API vertically, by getting a bigger server.

transcript.q: How does Kafka guarantee ordering?

transcript.a: Kafka guarantees global ordering across all partitions of a topic automatically, so you never need to think about keys or partitions.

transcript.close: Okay, thank you, that's the end.

cross_checks.why: Identical answers must score higher against a fresher bar than a senior bar.

consistency.why: Re-scoring the same interview should give nearly the same overall score.
